title: If AI Can Do It Better, Why Do It Yourself?
summary: AI coding tools can get a feature working, but the developer still might not know how to fix it. 3Blue1Brown's video and Anthropic's Trio study clarify the value of practice and enjoyment—yet whether you can practice on the clock depends on who owns that time.

title: Code Mode: Why Coding Agents Are Letting Models Write Code to Call Tools
summary: Code Mode lets coding agents put tool dependencies, error handling, and filtering into scripts, avoiding intermediate JSON overhead. Comparing Codex, Pi, OpenCode, and Claude Code, this post examines host boundaries with Bash, API stability, and the cost of non-rollback writes.

title: Agent Plans Start at the Database, So You Can't Try Anything Until the Last Layer
summary: Agent development plans, vertical slices: models tend to plan by database, service, API, and frontend, leaving nothing testable until the final layer. Switching to vertical slices lets you test each slice with curl or a browser as soon as it's done, with similar cuts for CLIs and libraries.

title: Agents Rarely Delete Code When Fixing Bugs, Just Layering Defenses On Top
summary: Agent bug fixes, code review, and AGENTS.md: when a fix diff only adds null checks and try-catch blocks, or keeps both options A and B, it often legalizes invalid states and pushes decisions onto future maintainers. Write three lines of default rules before delegating, and check deleted lines first during review.

title: Revenue Data from 10,000 Indie Products: AI Products Make Money at Almost the Same Rate as Non-AI
summary: Indie hacking and AI product revenue: across 10,150 products on TrustMRR, 49.3% of AI products have revenue vs. 49.0% of non-AI products, and only 2.41% make $100K a year. AI lowered the cost of building, not the odds that someone will pay.

title: Can't Get AI Code Review to Stop? Drop "Find Me a Bug" First
summary: AI code review, Claude Code, Codex: a PR ran through over fifty review rounds overnight, and roughly 59% of the recurring comments pointed to code already there in round one. The culprit is often the "find me a bug" prompt itself. Switching to neutral framing, requiring an issue count upfront, and capping review rounds helps break the loop.

title: Anthropic Merges 30,000 Changes a Day, and Git Broke First
summary: Git, CI, and merge queues: Anthropic's daily merges grew from 2,500 to 30,000, pushing them to migrate their monorepo off Git; GitHub saw over five times more commits in September than a year earlier. Most teams don't need to leave Git, but three changes are worth considering.

title: Personal Agent: After the Subsidies, Why Do Users Pay?
summary: Personal Agents are often compared to early Didi, but they lack ride-hailing's two-sided network effects—more users just mean bigger bills, and cloud startup credits do not cover third-party models. To judge the opportunity, look at whether a product can reliably finish a task users will pay for at a sustainable cost once subsidies end.

title: Can a Single Score Measure AI Code Quality?
summary: Line counts, duplication, and complexity can surface clues about AI slop, but a total score cannot replace maintenance judgment. Use metrics to locate problems, then watch how the code handles the next requirement change—otherwise you end up optimizing for good numbers by creating a different kind of bad code.

title: Why Agent Self-Improvement Doesn't Prove an Intelligence Explosion Yet
summary: Agent self-improvement experiments have shown gains in task performance, but evidence remains thin that an upgraded system can drive the next round of upgrades more efficiently. When reading Weco's experiment, distinguish higher task scores from a stronger capacity to improve.

title: Doing Research with OpenAI Can Also Mean Competing Against It
summary: The dispute between OpenAI and a mathematician over the Navier-Stokes equations exposes a harsher reality than data leaks: even without touching your private data, a model provider can become your direct competitor in the same race using stronger unreleased models and compute. Buying a tool is not forming an alliance, so you have to protect yourself with local version trails and dual-track isolation.

title: Why Stronger LLMs Make Code Review More Exhausting

The real metric for a model upgrade is how long you spend cleaning up after it declares the job done.

title: Does Everyone Using AI Make a Company AI-Native?
summary: An AI-native organization cannot be measured by account usage alone. Whether employees can access valid materials, whether working practices can be reused by colleagues, and whether someone owns failures determine if individual gains become part of the team's daily work.

title: Why Cheaper AI Code Means More Unnecessary Features
summary: When coding agents drive the marginal cost of writing code toward zero, the weakest link in the system becomes human mental bandwidth to say no. Edge requests that hand-coding costs once filtered out flood in, multiplying review and comprehension debt. What is scarce now is not code output, but the resolve to run git reset on spotless code.

What actually decides whether a product survives are two hard physical constraints set before starting: visitors must understand it in five seconds, and a solo maintainer must be able to afford keeping it up.

title: Infuse Subscription Migration - Exceptional Service from Firecore
summary: If you use Plex to manage your movies and TV shows, Infuse offers the best viewing experience on iPhone and Apple TV, and most users subscribe to unlock all features and future upgrades. Because the China region lacks an Apple TV App Store, my Chinese-region subscription wouldn't work on Apple TV, so I emailed support asking to transfer it to my Hong Kong account. After verifying my order, they sent me a promo code instead—leaving me with active subscriptions in both regions, with the Hong Kong term starting from redemption plus a free bonus month.
